St. Theodosius the Cenobiarch

St. Theodosius the Cenobiarch

St. Theodosius the Great

Period

Region
Holy Land
Titles / vocation

Introduction

St. Theodosius is the Cappadocian ascetic remembered for his large Palestinian community and defense of the Chalcedonian confession.

Background

The OCA describes his upbringing, church reading and singing, and journey to the Holy Land, including a meeting with Simeon the Stylite.

[1] Official Orthodox hagiographic account · Published biographical account,paragraph 1; Published biographical account,paragraph 2; Published biographical account,paragraph 3

CHEODOsius was born in Cappadocia in 423. The ex- ample of Abraham urged him to leave his country, and his desire to follow Jesus Christ attracted him to the religious life. He placed himself under Longinus, a very holy hermit, who sent him to govern a monastery near Bethlehem. Unable to bring himself to command others, he fled to a cavern, where he lived in penance and prayer. His great charity, however, forbade him to refuse the charge of some disciples, who, few at first, became in time a vast number, and Theodosius built a large monastery and three churches for them. He became eventually Su- perior of the religious communities of Palestine. Theo- dosius accommodated himself so carefully to the characters of his subjects that his reproofs were loved rather than dreaded.

Historical Roman Catholic compilation. OCR spelling and the source’s age calculation are retained; these differ from some Orthodox accounts.

[2] Historical biographical compilation · January 11, pp32–33, first part of the biographical narrative

Life and notable events

Disciples gather around his cave, and the life describes a monastery caring for travelers, the sick, and people in need.

[1] Official Orthodox hagiographic account · Published biographical account,paragraph 2; Published biographical account,paragraph 4; Published biographical account,paragraph 5

Theodosius never refused assistance to any in pov- erty or affliction; on some days the monks laid more than a hundred tables for those in want. In times of famine Theodosius forbade the alms to be diminished, and often miraculously multiplied the provisions. He also built five hospitals, in which he lovingly served the sick, while by assiduous spiritual reading he maintained himself in per- fect recollection. He successfully opposed the Eutychian heresy in Jerusalem, and for this was banished by the em- peror. He suffered a long and painful malady, and refused to pray to be cured, calling it a salutary penance for his former successes. He died at the age of a hundred and six.

The compilation’s historical biographical narrative; the separate devotional Reflection is not reproduced.

[2] Historical biographical compilation · January 11, p33, continuation before the separate Reflection

The official life distinguishes accommodation for strangers, infirmaries for monks and laypeople, and shelter for the dying. It describes Greek, Georgian, and Armenian services among a varied community, with the monks gathering together for Communion. It also places St. Theodosius’s opposition to imperial religious policy under Anastasius and reports temporary imprisonment. These are features of this Palestinian community’s published history.

[1] Official Orthodox hagiographic account · Published biographical account,paragraph 5; Published biographical account,paragraph 9

Death and martyrdom

The official account describes repose at an advanced age and burial in his original cave. It does not describe execution.

[1] Official Orthodox hagiographic account · Published biographical account,paragraph 6; Published biographical account,paragraph 9
